items.title: London to Tokyo flights cross Siberia — not because Russia is convenient
items.claim: On a flat map, the shortest path between London and Tokyo looks like a horizontal line through Central Asia. The ACTUAL shortest path on Earth's surface arcs north over Siberia. That's the great-circle route.
items.prompt: Why is the great-circle route shortest?

options.text: Any geodesic (shortest path) on a sphere is part of a great circle — a circle whose plane passes through the sphere's centre. Latitude lines (except the equator) are NOT great circles, so flying along a latitude isn't optimal

items.reveal:
A geodesic is the shortest path between two points on a surface. On a flat plane, geodesics are straight lines. On a sphere, geodesics are arcs of great circles — circles whose centre coincides with the sphere's centre.

All meridians (longitude lines, including the prime meridian and date line) are great circles. The equator is a great circle. Lines of latitude EXCEPT the equator are NOT great circles — they're small circles whose plane does not pass through Earth's centre.

London-Tokyo: separated by ~9600 km along the great-circle route, ~12000 km if you fly along the line of latitude (~50°N).

Map projections distort geodesics:
- Mercator projection (Gerardus Mercator, 1569): preserves angles (conformal), shows rhumb lines as straight, but distorts areas and great-circle paths.
- Gnomonic projection: shows great circles as straight lines, but is unsuitable as a navigational chart.
- Robinson, Mollweide: balance distortions in different ways.

Airlines plan routes along great circles, adjusted for winds (jetstream eastbound from US to Europe saves an hour). 'Polar' routes from North America to East Asia routinely cross the Arctic.

In general relativity, geodesics on curved spacetime trace the paths of free-falling objects — gravity IS geodesic motion through curved spacetime.
items.why: Maps lie about distances. Modern navigation requires understanding that the shortest path on a sphere is curved on a flat map. The intuition fails everywhere except locally.

items.title: The simplest population equation in the world becomes chaotic
items.claim: Logistic map: x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n). At r = 2.5, x converges to a fixed point. At r = 3.2, it oscillates between two values. At r = 3.7, the values look random. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.

options.text: Nothing — the system is always periodic

Period-doubling cascade: a single fixed point splits into a 2-cycle, then a 4-cycle, then 8, 16, 32... at geometrically closer values of r (Feigenbaum's constant ~4.669). Beyond ~3.5699, the system becomes chaotic
Only mathematicians can see the difference
The chaos is a calculation error

items.reveal_title: Period doubling and the road to chaos
items.reveal:
The logistic map x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n) was introduced by Robert May (1976) as a simple model of population growth with carrying capacity.

For r between 0 and 1: x converges to 0.
For r between 1 and 3: x converges to a non-zero fixed point.
At r = 3: the fixed point becomes unstable; period-2 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.449: period-4 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.544: period-8.
At r ≈ 3.5644: period-16.

The period-doublings occur at geometrically closer r-values, with ratio approaching Feigenbaum's constant delta ≈ 4.669 — a universal constant of period-doubling bifurcations, appearing in many physical systems (dripping faucet, electronic circuits, fluid dynamics).

At r ≈ 3.5699: 'Edge of chaos'. Beyond this, the system becomes chaotic — small differences in initial conditions grow exponentially.

Within the chaos there are 'islands of stability' (e.g., a period-3 window near r ≈ 3.83). The bifurcation diagram has fractal structure.

This system shows that deterministic dynamics can produce apparent randomness. It motivated chaos theory in the 1970s-80s.

Applications:
- Population biology (when not too realistic).
- Cryptography (pseudo-random number generators).
- Modelling complex systems (transitions to turbulence).
- Analogies to neural and economic dynamics.

The logistic map is a foundational example in the study of dynamical systems and has become a textbook reference for chaos.
items.why: Even the simplest equations can produce unpredictable behaviour. Determinism doesn't guarantee predictability — chaos can emerge from one-line iterations. This insight overturned 19th-century certainty about Newtonian mechanics.

items.title: 1 is the first digit of natural numbers 30% of the time
items.claim: Take any 'natural' set of numbers — house prices, river lengths, populations, physical constants. Look at the first digit. About 30% start with 1. Only 4.6% start with 9. The pattern is so reliable that auditors use it to detect fraud.

options.text: Benford's law: for scale-invariant distributions, the probability of first digit d is log10(1 + 1/d). The math reflects that doubling a number (or scaling by any factor) takes longer to pass through 1-2 than through 8-9 on a logarithmic axis

items.reveal:
Simon Newcomb (1881) noticed that the early pages of his logarithm tables (corresponding to leading digit 1) were more worn than the later pages. He inferred something about how often various leading digits appeared.

Frank Benford (1938, physicist) systematically tested the rule across many datasets (river lengths, populations, atomic weights, baseball stats, addresses). He found:
Digit 1: 30.1%
Digit 2: 17.6%
Digit 3: 12.5%
Digit 4: 9.7%
Digit 5: 7.9%
Digit 6: 6.7%
Digit 7: 5.8%
Digit 8: 5.1%
Digit 9: 4.6%
Formula: P(d) = log10(1 + 1/d).

Why: many natural quantities span multiple orders of magnitude. On a logarithmic scale, the spacing from 1 to 2 (log 2 ≈ 0.30) is much wider than from 9 to 10 (log 10/9 ≈ 0.046). If the distribution is roughly uniform in log space, leading digits follow Benford.

Applications:
- Forensic accounting: real financial data follow Benford; fabricated numbers usually don't. Auditors flag tax returns or financial statements that deviate.
- Election fraud detection: ballot counts in honest elections follow Benford; many disputed elections have shown deviations.
- Scientific fraud detection: many cases of data fabrication caught.
- Image authenticity: pixel JPEG coefficients follow Benford-like distributions; fakes often don't.

Limitations: Benford requires scale-invariant data spanning multiple orders of magnitude. Constrained data (height, ages) don't satisfy it. Carefully fabricated data designed to fool Benford also exist.

The mathematical generalisation: any distribution with logarithmic density invariant under scaling will produce Benford's law for leading digits.
items.why: Random-looking data often follow precise patterns. Benford's law is counterintuitive and has practical applications in fraud detection. It's also a window into how scale-invariance shapes the structure of numbers we encounter.
